title: Heat, Airflow, and Cooling
summary: Interpret synthetic thermal data and connect temperature patterns to airflow and workload clues.
objectives: Explain how workload and airflow affect temperature.
Interpret simulated temperature data and identify a safe next investigation.

vocab.def: Movement of thermal energy from one place or material to another.
An area with higher-than-expected temperature in a system.
Heat produced by equipment or work that a cooling design must manage.

sections.heading: Work creates thermal load
sections.body: Computing uses energy and produces heat. More work can change the thermal load. Cooling design uses airflow, temperature monitoring, and equipment arrangement to manage that heat.

sections.heading: Read the pattern
sections.body: A single hot reading, a rising trend, and several hot zones suggest different questions. A blocked intake, a workload change, or a sensor issue may be possible causes.

sections.heading: Use synthetic data
sections.body: Analyze a provided temperature table or simulation. Do not service HVAC equipment, open energized hardware, or treat one classroom threshold as universal operational guidance.

practice.prompt: A rack temperature rises from 22 to 28 degrees while nearby racks stay stable. Calculate the change and name two safe questions to investigate.

quiz.question: What is a useful first response to a simulated rising temperature trend?
options: Record the evidence and investigate airflow, workload, and sensor context
Change a building HVAC setting without permission
quiz.answer: Record the evidence and investigate airflow, workload, and sensor context

lab.objective: Interpret synthetic temperature readings and identify a likely next investigation.

futureCompetencyCandidates: relate temperature patterns to possible system causes
reflectionPrompt: What additional measurement would make a thermal conclusion more trustworthy?
